title: 17 Maxims for a Good Life
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: Writing as Antonius Veritas, the Stoic Manual author offers seventeen aphorisms meant to make a reader smarter, more effective, respected and happier. The maxims move from the Stoic view that a good life rests on wisdom, courage, justice and self-control, through advice on learning, being valuable as well as well-connected, and setting bold ambitions. They continue with counsel on manners, reputation, patience in revealing one's abilities, and prudent use of imagination. Several concern working with others: persuasion requires knowing what moves each person, and helping people reach their deepest desires wins their hearts. The closing maxims warn against dispersing effort across many goals and urge turning bad news into forward action. The collection is a compact, practical guide to character and professional presence for leaders.
points: Do not make happiness depend on money, recognition or affection, since each involves conditions you cannot fully control; the Stoics located the good life in wisdom, courage, justice and self-control.
Being a person of value matters more than being well-connected, but the best course is to be both, and keep learning, refining your craft and helping others.
Bold, uncomfortable ambitions force you to acquire ancillary skills such as leadership, public speaking, listening and emotional control.
Let people discover your abilities over time, since a problem handled well leaves a stronger impression than a catalogue of achievements.
Persuasion depends on knowing what moves each person, and focusing on one goal at a time protects the quality of your work.
quotes: Learning asks you to endure the discovery that you know less than you thought. Ask the question anyway.
The embarrassment of being a beginner passes. But the cost of pretending you already know keeps growing.
It's thus much better to be a man of value than well-connected, but best to be both.
Keep learning. Work on your weaknesses. Refine your craft. Aim for excellence. Be genuine in helping others with problems aligning with your expertise.
You can take an attempt seriously without making its initial outcome a judgment on your entire future. There is still another version to make. Another rep. And another idea to try.

You can allow people to discover your abilities over time. A thoughtful observation, a problem handled well, or an unexpected skill often leaves a stronger impression than a prattled catalogue of achievements.
Success in persuasion requires knowing what moves each person. Common needs are ease, status, pleasure, and money but mostly connection and a good time.
Focusing on many goals disperses the potential of doing one well. It's thus wise to try one thing before moving on to another.
